newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Tunis bourse looks to automated trading, new rules.
newsitem.headline: Tunis bourse looks to automated trading, new rules.

text.p: The Tunisian Stock Exchange hopes to start trading with a computerised dealing system next month under new regulations aimed at attracting more private capital and company listings to this North African share market.

"We are technically ready to start by October. It is now up to brokers to be ready to use the new dealing software by that deadline," Mohamed Hadouej, head of the brokers-managed Tunis Stock Exchange told Reuters.
Finance Minister Nouri Zorgati met stockbrokers over the weekend and urged them to be ready for the new dealing system and regulations by next month.
He also told them to encourage companies to list on the bourse, adding the aim was to have 100 listed firms compared with 30 today.
"We are ready for a start with the new dealing system by October 21," said brokers' association president Hamza Knani.
The Tunis bourse, with a turnover in 1995 of 918 million dinars ($890 million) and a capitalisation of 3.66 billion dinars, trades through displaying prices on notice boards.
By the time the new dealing system goes live, the bourse will also have implemented new regulations which officials and brokers say will boost the number of listed firms.
The 64-page "Reglement General" -- which still has to be signed by the finance minister -- eases listing conditions and establishes a guarantee fund.
Firms are no longer required to have a minimum one million dinars in capital to be listed on the primary market or a minimum of 500,000 dinars for the secondary market.

Instead, they must sell a minimum 20 percent of their capital to at least 500 shareholders to be listed on the primary market and 10 percent to at least 300 shareholders to be listed on the secondary market through public share offers.

"The new rules of admission will enable a score of Tunisian firms...to open themselves to the bourse," said Mohamed Salah H'Maidi, head of the Financial Market Council, the bourse's regulatory watchdog.
The guarantee fund, to be financed by contributions from brokers, guarantees the payment of transactions when a broker fails to honour his commitment.

"What I expect is that the new dealing system will obviously introduce more transparency and therefore investors will be better informed," said Paul-Francois Dubroeucq, head of the Paris bourse team which set up the system funded by French government aid.
Brokers welcomed the new regulations as they would give more protection to investors.
"We are satisfied with the text in general, but we need to see how the dealing software works to see how to adapt," said Nejib Hajri, director of broker Societe Financiere de Gestion.
